## Overview

Section 4.3 of Diekmann, Heesterbeek and Roberts (2010) is a model of bovine viral
diarrhoea (BVD). Cattle infected horizontally pass through an exposed (`E`) and a transiently
infectious (`I`) stage. A fraction `p₁` of those recovering while pregnant carry an infected
foetus (`Z`, immune themselves), and with probability `p₂` the calf is born *persistently
infected* (`P`): highly infectious for life (shortened by `b`), and itself giving birth to
persistently infected calves at a reduced rate `μ - a`. There are therefore two
states-at-infection, `E` and `P`, and `K` is `2 × 2` with a non-zero diagonal, which exercises
the full quadratic closed form.

As in vignette 8, the paper gives only the infected subsystem; the full model below adds a
susceptible class with balanced births and deaths.

## The model

```{julia}
using ReproductiveNumbers, ModelingToolkit, Symbolics
using ModelingToolkit: t_nounits as t, D_nounits as D

@parameters β₁ β₂ ν γ μ p₁ p₂ α a b N
@variables S(t) E(t) I(t) Z(t) P(t) R(t)
horizontal = S * (β₁ * I + β₂ * P) / N
eqs = [D(S) ~ μ * N - horizontal - μ * S,
       D(E) ~ horizontal - (ν + μ) * E,
       D(I) ~ ν * E - (γ + μ) * I,
       D(Z) ~ p₁ * γ * I - (α + μ) * Z,
       D(P) ~ p₂ * α * Z + (μ - a) * P - (μ + b) * P,
       D(R) ~ (1 - p₁) * γ * I + α * Z - μ * R]
bvd = complete(System(eqs, t; name = :bvd))
```

Three kinds of event create a new infected animal: horizontal infection (into `E`), the
birth of a persistently infected calf from a `Z` cow (`p₂ α Z`), and the birth of a
persistently infected calf from a `P` cow (`(μ - a) P`). The transition `I → Z` is *not* a
transmission: the foetus is counted when it is born.

```{julia}
ngm = next_generation_matrix(bvd, [E, I, Z, P];
                             transmission = [horizontal, 0, 0, p₂ * α * Z + (μ - a) * P])
```

## The next-generation matrix

```{julia}
states_at_infection(ngm), ngm.K
```

Reading the entries: `K[1, 1]` is the number of horizontal infections caused by one
exposed animal that survives latency and is infectious for `1/(γ + μ)`; `K[1, 2]` those
caused by a persistently infected animal over its life `1/(μ + b)`; `K[2, 1]` is the
probability that an exposed animal produces a persistently infected calf; and `K[2, 2]` the
number of persistently infected calves born to one persistently infected animal.

```{julia}
R0 = basic_reproduction_number(ngm)
```

## Two routes to persistence

```{julia}
vals = Dict(β₁ => 0.5, β₂ => 5.0, ν => 0.2, γ => 0.1, μ => 0.003, p₁ => 0.3, p₂ => 0.5,
            α => 0.01, a => 0.001, b => 0.01, N => 1000.0)
num = evaluate(ngm, vals)
(basic_reproduction_number(num), num.K)
```

Type reproduction numbers separate the contributions: `T_E` is the number of horizontal
infections traced back to one horizontal infection through any number of persistently
infected generations, and `T_P` the same for the persistently infected type. Removing all
persistently infected animals at birth eliminates the infection only if `T_P` exceeds one
and `K[1,1]` is below one:

```{julia}
(type_reproduction_number(num, E), type_reproduction_number(num, P), num.K[1, 1])
```

```{julia}
elasticities(ngm, vals; params = [β₁, β₂, p₁, p₂, b])
```
